# Systematic errors of human judgement (cognitive biases) (`cognitive_biases`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by controlled_trial
- Core idea: Human minds err in predictable directions: we notice and remember what confirms our belief (confirmation bias), see patterns and intentions in chance, judge frequency by vivid cases, anchor on the first number heard, and explain away our own failures. Being clever or honest does not protect anyone, which is why methods that do not rely on judgement are needed: write predictions down beforehand, count hits and misses, use controls and blinding, and invite an opponent to check. A quick demonstration is Wason's game: say that 2, 4, 6 follows a secret rule and let people test triples; many people try only cases that fit their guess and overlook rules that also fit those cases.
- Pitfalls:
  - Believing that knowing about biases makes one immune; people readily see them in others only
  - Using 'you are biased' as an insult or a way to end an argument
  - Repeating famous findings that later failed replication (several social-priming results popularised in the 2000s)
  - Presenting a tidy catalogue of hundreds of named biases as settled science; the solid core is small
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Thucydides notes that people accept what they wish and reason away what they dislike; china: c. 250 BC – Xunzi, 'Dispelling Blindness', on how a partial view obscures the whole; india: early centuries AD – Nyaya Sutras list fallacious reasons and sophistical moves in debate; islamic: 1377 – Ibn Khaldun lists the causes of error in reports: partisanship, trust in transmitters, flattery of the powerful, ignorance of how things work; europe: 1620 – Bacon's four 'idols' of the mind; 1960 Wason's 2-4-6 task; 1974 Tversky & Kahneman, heuristics and biases
- Read:
  - Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620)
  - Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974)
  - Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)
